story_type: first shuttle launch after a disaster, onboard tank camera
hook: The first shuttle to fly after Columbia was lost.
narration: This was the first space shuttle to launch after Columbia was lost.
Discovery, July twenty sixth, two thousand five, from Launch Pad 39B in Florida.
Columbia was lost in February two thousand three. For nearly two and a half years, no shuttle flew.
Seven astronauts rode up on this one to test new ways to inspect and repair a shuttle in orbit.
Columbia was destroyed when hot gas got in through a damaged panel on its wing. So this time, a camera on the orange fuel tank watched the orbiter the whole way up.
About two minutes in, the two solid rocket boosters burned out.
[short pause] Then they let go and fell away.
outcome: Discovery made it to space, and fourteen days later it landed safely in California.
title: First shuttle to fly after Columbia
description:
On July 26, 2005, Space Shuttle Discovery launched from Pad 39B at Kennedy Space Center on STS-114, the first shuttle flight since the loss of Columbia in February 2003. Fourteen days later it landed safely at Edwards Air Force Base, California.

extra_sources.excerpt: This is the first Space Shuttle flight since the loss of Columbia, STS-107, on Feb. 1, 2003.

The STS-114 landing concluded a historic 14 day return to flight mission to the International Space Station (ISS) after nearly a two and one half year delay in flight after the Space Shuttle Columbia tragedy in February 2003.
During its 12-day mission, Discovery’s seven-person crew will test new hardware and techniques to improve Shuttle safety, as well as deliver supplies to the International Space Station.
Discovery spent two weeks in space, where the crew demonstrated new methods to inspect and repair the Shuttle in orbit.
Following the Columbia accident in February 2002, which was caused by a breach in an RCC panel that allowed hot gases into the vehicle, each panel on Discovery was removed and thoroughly inspected

Space Shuttle Discovery landed safely at NASA's Dryden Flight Research Center at Edwards Air Force Base in Calif. at 5:11:22 a.m. PDT this morning, following the very successful 14-day STS-114 return to flight mission.
